Empirical Research Plan – “Ranking Schools on Noisy Test Scores”

---------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), augmented with a difference-in-discontinuity (DiD-RD) panel extension.

Why RDD?  
• The policy introduces a sharp cutoff in the ranking distribution (e.g., schools above the 75th percentile receive awards / lenient inspections; those below do not).  
• Schools located just above and below the cutoff are plausibly comparable on all pre-treatment characteristics except the treatment itself.  
• The ranking is a deterministic function of the running variable (the test-score index), so assignment is “as-good-as-random” in an infinitesimal neighborhood of the cutoff.  
• Multiple years allow us to difference-out any permanent school-level unobservables and to verify pre-trend balance.

Why not pure DID? The key variation is cross-sectional (just-above vs. just-below the threshold) rather than a clearly exogenous policy stagger.  
Why not IV? The cutoff itself is the assignment mechanism, not an instrument for another endogenous treatment.

---------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
---------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_it = 1 if the (de-meaned) school-year average test score s_it ≥ cutoff c in year t, 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Schools in a narrow bandwidth h on the left of the cutoff (c – h ≤ s_it < c).

Treatment timing  
Treatment starts the academic year immediately after rankings are published. For year t scores (collected in spring), the intervention is implemented in fall of t+1. We therefore measure outcomes Y_{i,t+1} (or longer-run T+2, T+3 effects).

Running variable and cutoff  
Running variable: standardized school-level test-score index s_it.  
Cutoff: official threshold c_t (can vary by grade cohort or year; treat as time-varying). If c_t changes discretely, we re-center scores each year: ũ_it = s_it – c_t.

Bandwidth choice will follow Calonico-Cattaneo-Farrell (2014) MSE-optimal bandwidth and robustness to ±25% of that.

Panel extension  
Because we have multiple pre-policy cohorts, we also estimate a difference-in-discontinuity:

(Y_{it} – Y_{it-1}) = α + τ·TREAT_it + f(ũ_it) + f(ũ_{it})·POST_t + ε_it

where POST_t = 1 for years after the ranking system started.

---------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
---------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff  
Absent the treatment, schools just above/below c would have had identical mean outcomes. Plausibility: high—schools are ranked solely on noisy averaged scores; parents, budgets, teacher contracts are locked-in for next school year.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable  
Schools cannot “stuff” scores to move across the threshold within a few points. External proctoring and standardized grading bolster this.

A3. Correct functional form / bandwidth choice  
Local linear / quadratic controls with optimal bandwidth capture smooth trends.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers)  
Outcomes of one school are not shifted by neighboring schools marginally crossing the cutoff. Reasonable because interventions are school-specific (funding, audits).

A5. Parallel trends for DiD-RD  
For the difference-in-discontinuity, differences just above vs. below in pre-policy years must be flat. Testable in pre-period.

---------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
---------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Score manipulation (gaming)  
• McCrary density test on running variable.  
• Placebo thresholds away from c.  
• Manual audit of outliers; robustness dropping suspected cheaters.

Threat 2: Sorting of students across schools after rankings are published  
• Use outcomes measured in the year immediately after treatment, before large re-sorting can occur.  
• Test balance on lagged enrollment and demographic composition within bandwidth.  
• Re-estimate restricting to schools with stable enrollment (<±5 % change).

Threat 3: Mean-reversion in noisy test scores (regression to the mean)  
• Difference-in-discontinuity removes mean-reversion bias by netting out pre-treatment outcomes.  
• Use instrumental variables RD (rank eligibility as instrument for actual intervention receipt) if compliance <100 %.

---------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
---------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ----- 0. Packages -----
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # for feols
library(rdrobust)    # Calonico et al. RD
library(rddensity)   # McCrary test

# ----- 1. Load data -----
df <- read_csv("school_rank_data.csv")

# ----- 2. Construct variables -----
df <- df %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(
    centered_score = test_score - cutoff,   # running variable ũ_it
    treat          = if_else(centered_score >= 0, 1, 0),
    post_policy    = if_else(year >= policy_start_year, 1, 0),
    outcome_next   = lead(outcome, 1)       # outcome in t+1
  ) %>% ungroup()

# Restrict analysis window (pre-specify ±3 SD to speed later bw choice)
df <- df %>% filter(abs(centered_score) <= 3)

# ----- 3. Main sharp RD (cross-sectional) -----
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_next, x = df$centered_score,
                    c = 0, p = 1, kernel = "triangular")
summary(rd_main)

# ----- 4. Difference-in-discontinuity panel RD -----
# First create outcome change
df <- df %>%
  arrange(school_id, year) %>%
  group_by(school_id) %>%
  mutate(delta_outcome = outcome_next - lag(outcome_next)) %>%
  ungroup()

did_rd <- feols(delta_outcome ~ treat*post_policy + f(centered_score, 1) |
                  school_id + year, data = df, subset = abs(centered_score) < 2)
summary(did_rd)

# ----- 5. Density manipulation test -----
rddensity(df$centered_score, c = 0)

# ----- 6. Robustness: alternative bandwidth (±25%) -----
h_opt <- rd_main$bws[1,1]
for(h in c(0.75,1,1.25)*h_opt){
  tmp <- rdrobust(df$outcome_next, df$centered_score, h = h, c = 0)
  print(paste("Bandwidth:", round(h,3), "Point estimate:", tmp$coef[1]))
}

```

---------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
---------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition suggests a small positive effect of being above the cutoff: additional resources, prestige, or lighter regulatory scrutiny may improve subsequent test outcomes by 0.03–0.05 SD. However, because rankings are based on noisy scores, part of the discontinuity could be mean-reversion, so the “true” causal effect may be closer to 0.02 SD.

---------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (sharp RD)
---------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Clear, known cutoff – 1  
C2: Running variable not manipulated – 0.8 (some risk of gaming)  
C3: Covariate balance around cutoff – 0.9  
C4: No other discontinuous polices at cutoff – 1  
C5: Bandwidth robustness / functional-form stability – 0.9  

Total ≈ 4.6 / 5 → high credibility with stated caveats.
